doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Benny Carter's Further Definitions, Newport with Hawkins and Bob Prince's saxophone album
summary: Identifying a Carter session, earlier work with its players, Newport with Hawkins, and the Warner sax album where Hawkins played one take.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Let me ask you, well I don’t mean ask you, I said I’m going to pick out one thing that you played on and just bring it with me. It’s a hard thing, when you’ve played on so many recordings. But —
And I want you to just see if you — maybe you won’t even recognize what it is.
Yeah I know what that is. That’s Benny Carter’s “Further Definitions.” What is that “Crazy Rhythm?”
Oh I’ll tell you an anecdote connected with this record, that I’m very proud of. You must have a newer — is this the two—
I’ll show you the album later.
Is this the one that has the other one in it too?

Yeah I’d like to see if it’s the same one I have because that piano sounds better here than it does on mine. Anyhow during that record date, I don’t even know how I got on the date because I hadn’t met Benny Carter before then. I knew everybody else in the band, except John Collins, I didn’t know him, but I had played with Jimmy Garrison, with Philly Joe, I had worked with Jo Jones a lot, I worked with Phil Woods, I worked with his group with Gene Quill. And Charlie Rouse I don’t know if I’d ever worked with but probably jammed with him or something. Who else is one there? And Coleman Hawkins I had played with. I played with Coleman Hawkins at Newport the first time. J.J., Coleman Hawkins and Buck Clayton.

Yeah. George Avakian put that together on the spur of the moment. And also there is a very obscure album which should be reissued. Warner Brothers is doing some jazz in the late 50s or early 60s, and there was this guy named Bob Prince, an arranger, and he did these two oddball albums. One was — I think it was twelve trombones or something, it was all trombones. Then there’s one that’s called Saxophones Incorporated, and it was twelve saxophones I think. And it sounded like a big band. You didn’t even miss the brass the way he arranged it. And every guy in it was a hotshot. And I remember Georgie Auld played on it and Coleman Hawkins came in to do a feature. And there is an interesting story that goes with this because the arranger, Bob Prince, Coleman didn’t have to read or anything, they just said, “What do you want to play on this record, your featured solo, I’ll write the arrangement around whatever you want to do.” And he says, “Well how about ‘The Gypsy?’” You know that song? I think Bird was playing it. And Bob Prince didn’t know it, so he asked Coleman to sing it to him. So when Coleman sang it he sang the bridge in long meter, it was twice as many bars, and that’s the way he arranged it. It came out great. So Coleman came in, I’ll never forget it, and it hat on — he played one take. Flawless. He said, “Can I hear that back? Okay. Thanks a lot fellas, bye.” Walked out. That was that. I never seen that happen before. Usually everybody’s sweating over it. So that was a nice record. It almost disappeared. You wanted to ask me a question about that? Or you just wanted to do the blindfold test?
No, I just wanted to see if you remembered it, and if it was a good date for you.
Oh, the story that goes with that date. It was very relaxed and I remember Coleman, I think he might have been wearing a tux because he was working in the Metropole or
